subject: Cognitive Science
title: Status Quo Bias
description: A micro-lesson that makes Status Quo Bias usable.

hook.text: Countries with opt-out organ donation have 90% donors. Opt-in countries? About 15%. Same people, different default.

buildup.text: Status quo bias: people prefer the current state of affairs, even when change would benefit them.

discovery.text: Samuelson and Zeckhauser showed it in 1988: people stick with inherited investment plans regardless of quality.

twist.text: Defaults are extraordinarily powerful. Whoever sets the default often controls the decision.

climax.text: Inertia isn't laziness—it's the brain conserving effort. Change requires energy; staying put is free.

punchline.text: The easiest choice is no choice. That's the trap.

quiz.question: Why is the status quo bias powerful?

details.summary: People prefer the current state of affairs and resist change even when better alternatives exist. This status quo bias combines loss aversion, endowment effects, and simple inertia. Default options in policy, technology, and finance exploit this tendency with enormous consequences.
details.whyItMatters: Status quo bias explains why bad policies persist, why people stick with suboptimal defaults, and why change is so difficult even when the benefits are clear.
takeaways: People prefer the current state even when alternatives are better
Loss aversion and inertia reinforce the status quo
Default options exploit this bias in policy and design

faq.question: How do default options exploit status quo bias?
faq.answer: Making organ donation opt-out rather than opt-in increased participation from around 15 percent to over 85 percent in some countries. The same principle applies to retirement savings defaults, privacy settings, and subscription renewals. Defaults are immensely powerful because of status quo bias.

faq.question: Is status quo bias always irrational?
faq.answer: Not always. The current state has been tested by experience, and switching involves real costs and uncertainty. Status quo bias becomes irrational when the evidence clearly favors change but people resist anyway due to comfort, fear, or loss aversion rather than rational evaluation.
